A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Reducio-VAE/Reducio-DiT work, with matching methods and experiments that support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 adds readable Appendices A and B.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.3 report original video reconstruction, generation, efficiency and ablation results.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds a human preference study, recursive generation examples and further experimental comparisons and ablations.

M1.justification: v3 Section 4.2 introduces recursive inference: the last generated frame conditions the next clip, enabling 32- and 48-frame outputs. The core conditioned VAE, DiT architecture, compression settings and progressive training procedure remain unchanged. Newly documented implementation details do not establish further method changes.

E1.justification: The Pexels/internal training data and Pexels, UCF-101, MSR-VTT and VBench evaluation coverage remain. v3 adds zero-shot continuation across multiple clips, where generated output becomes the subsequent condition, extending the demonstrated scenario beyond v1's single 16-frame clips.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds quantitative image-to-video comparisons with VideoComposer, I2VGen-XL and DynamiCrafter; v1 compared DynamiCrafter visually. Table 12 adds DC-AE, while Tables 14–15 substantially expand VBench comparisons, including Pyramid Flow, WAN, STIV and CausVid. The original main reconstruction and text-to-video comparator sets remain.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a 20-participant study of 15 video groups, using identical PixArt-α-1024 condition images and three preference criteria. It also adds a 512×512 Pexels comparison with DC-AE. Table 1 revises the reported SDXL-VAE latent channels from 16 to 4, without establishing reruns. The original training budgets and 20-step sampling setting remain.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds convolution-type and random-versus-middle content-frame ablations (Tables 10–11), extending tests of central design choices. Figures 7 and 12 add longer-generation and qualitative comparison cases; one urban reconstruction example is removed from Figure 4. The attention-type ablation moves unchanged from v1 Table 7 to v3 Table 13, and existing unconditioned/middle-frame results are reused.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests for its empirical results. The new human preference percentages are point results without uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Matched main reconstruction, generation and original ablation scores remain unchanged, but v3 adds substantial comparison and analysis results. New findings include 64% visual-quality and 57% content-alignment preference, and WAN/CausVid VBench totals of 83.96/83.88 above Reducio's retained 81.39. Table 2 places Reducio ahead of DynamiCrafter on UCF-101 but behind on MSR-VTT. MicroCinema's reported training cost changes from >25K to >6K A100 hours.

T1.justification: v3 removes the explicit reverse-diffusion formulation, noise-prediction loss and conditioning equations from v1 Section 3.2, Equations 1–3. The latent-shape and compression definitions remain. No new theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: image-conditioned motion latents, the claimed 64× compression relative to a common 2D VAE, and efficient Reducio-DiT generation. The headline claims of approximately 3.2K A100 training hours and 15.5-second generation of 16-frame 1K videos remain.

C2.justification: v3 shifts the limitations discussion from one-second outputs toward short training clips, limited training data and instruction-following limitations. It adds failure conditions involving entities absent from the content frame and explains the middle frame's temporal centrality. Appendix B acknowledges stronger WAN/CausVid scores while emphasizing Reducio's smaller data and model budgets.

D1.justification: Appendix A and Section 3.1 add VAE architecture and loss details, a 4e-5 learning rate, one million iterations, guidance scale 2.5, condition dropout, and tiling, overlap, blending and padding instructions. v3 also discloses LLaVA-1.5 captioning and clarifies timing and training-cost scope. Initialization remains ambiguous because the new pretrained-initialization discussion is not reconciled with the retained from-scratch training statement.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of CausVid's distillation approach and updates citations across video and visual generation. Appendix B adds positioning against DC-AE, WAN and CausVid. The central relationship to LaMD, PVDM and CMD, including the emphasis on aggressive spatial compression, remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract and selected method/result paragraphs, distinguishes image-to-video and factorized text-to-video evaluation more clearly, and moves the attention ablation into an appendix. The main section order and much prose remain. The title abbreviates 1024×1024 to 1K, affiliations are updated, and the introductory quotation is removed.

P2.justification: v3 adds preference and recursive-generation figures, detailed architecture diagrams, additional visual comparisons, and new comparison, hyperparameter and ablation tables. Existing displays are also rearranged: Figure 4 becomes a smaller two-case display, Figure 5 loses its reference-image panel beside the new preference plot, and the attention table moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's selected image-to-video visual examples and brief VAE training description, v3 provides stronger quantitative and human validation, broader baseline context and useful implementation details. These improve support and reproducibility, but reporting problems limit the gain: initialization remains ambiguous, Table 10 states fs=64 while its text states fs=32, and Table 2's 429.2 versus 318.5 does not support the claimed 90-point gap.
